transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-13
Time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Nair (Redwood); Evan Torres, Marisol Reyes, Jon Park (Saffron AI)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Alex walked through cost levers, Priya answered infra/benchmark questions. Saffron clarified a strict monthly inference budget and need for <100ms p90 for customer-facing prompts. Discussion touched on batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization, and private deployment constraints (KMS, on-prem). Agreed on pilot.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for making time, um this is Alex from Redwood, with Priya — she's our system engineer — we'll run through the per-call cost model and then dig into your traffic and budget constraints. how's that sound?
[00:12] Evan (Saffron CTO): yeah sounds good, thanks. quick context — we're on a pretty tight monthly inference spend, around $8k-12k for the first quarter, and aiming to ship a conversational assistant that sees bursts up to ~40 QPS. latency target p90 under 150ms ideally under 100ms for short queries.
[00:30] Priya (Redwood SE): got it, thanks evan. just to calibrate, when you say 'conversational assistant' — are we seeing a lot of prefix reuse? do many queries start with the same system prompt or user templates?
[00:45] Marisol (ML Eng): yeah many start with a shared system prompt + user intent slot, like 60% of calls have the same 120-token system prefix, then a short 20-80 token user message. plus some longer sequences for follow-ups.
[01:02] Alex: perfect, that's the sweet spot for prefix caching. so the main levers we'll talk about: per-token pricing (hosted API), batching window and throughput, KV/prefix cache hit rate, quantization level (4-bit/8-bit), and hosting mode — hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[01:20] Jon (Ops): quick question — when you say 'per-token', do you price generated tokens differently than input tokens? how does Redwood do that?
[01:30] Alex: good question. our hosted pricing has separate units for prompt tokens and completion tokens in the billing model; typical examples customers see are $X per 1k prompt tokens, $Y per 1k completion tokens — the spreadsheet i'll share breaks down both. for dedicated and private we move to committed capacity + per-node cost which we translate back to per-token equivalents using batch/throughput projections.
[01:52] Evan: can you talk about how batching reduces unit cost? our worry is increased latency if we batch too aggressively.
[02:00] Priya: absolutely. batching increases GPU utilization by grouping concurrent requests into one forward pass — if you have bursts of concurrent short requests, you can see 2x-8x token-cost reductions. the tradeoff is added queuing delay: if you set a 20ms batching window you'll see minimal latency impact but less batching, if you go to a 50-100ms window you can pick up more efficiency. we usually recommend adaptive batching with latency SLOs — e.g., keep p95 under your limit and let the system expand batch size when queueing won't violate SLO.
[02:34] Marisol: hmm adaptive sounds good but we have customers who are very latency-sensitive. Is there a way to prioritize routes?
[02:40] Alex: yes, routing by policy is supported — you can pin high-priority prompts to lowest-latency pools (dedicated or hosted low-latency cluster) and send lower-priority background tasks to cheap high-batch pools. that is, you can mix hosting modes logically even within one account by route.
[02:55] [00:03:00] Evan: we heard dedicated can get much lower cost per token at scale — what thresholds should we be thinking about?
[03:06] Priya: for predictable throughput and committed usage, dedicated becomes cost-effective when sustained QPS is high enough to keep GPU utilization above ~40-50% after your batching profile and KV cache benefits. ballpark: if you're in the tens of millions of tokens/month definitely worth evaluating dedicated. but it depends on model size/quant and your cache hit rate. if you have high prefix reuse (like you said, ~60%) effective tokens per call drop a lot which makes dedicated more attractive earlier.
[03:38] Jon: we also have compliance asks — customer data must remain in our VPC and all keys managed by our KMS. does Redwood support that?
[03:46] Alex: yep that's our Private offering — you get a customer-managed control plane, KMS integration, and optional on-prem package if you need air-gap. private is priced as an enterprise license + infra and support. we can include SS, SOC 2 docs — i'll attach the security pack.
[04:02] Marisol: okay noted. let's go into the math a bit — can you show an example per-call for our median request: 120-token prompt prefix + 40-token user + 60-token completion?
[04:12] Priya: sure. raw tokens = prompt 160 (prompt includes system+user) + completion 60 = 220 tokens total. with a 60% prefix cache hit rate your effective prompt token billable drops to: cached prefix (120 tokens) at 60% -> only billing the 40 tokens non-cached for those calls. i'll spit out a sample: average billed tokens per call ~ 100-120 depending on hit rate and quant/packing efficiency. then multiply by hosted rate. in dedicated we'd translate to tokens via throughput model — e.g., a single GPU at 7B q4 might do X tokens/s which maps to $/token when amortized over infra and infra utilization. i'll add concrete numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:00] Evan: can you be explicit about worst-case latency when you do batching plus prefetched KV cache? some caches are in memory and very fast but if you miss it could add overhead.
[05:12] Priya: KV cache hit is usually just memory lookup — single-digit ms. misses add the full forward pass cost. our runtime keeps a small in-GPU KV cache to avoid memory copies, but there are edge cases if you cross shards. for worst-case we assume cold KV miss plus small batch overhead — that can push p90 to model inference time + ~20-40ms depending on device.
[05:40] Marisol: and quantization — how risky is going to 4-bit for generation quality? we can't tolerate hallucination regressions.
[05:49] Alex: quality varies by model and prompt. Redwood Optimize includes recommended quantization profiles per workload and a preflight eval. many customers use q4f16 or similar to get most of the speed/cost gains with minimal quality loss; we can run your prompt set through a gate check: if we detect >X% metric regression we fall back to higher-precision variant. this is part of the SOW for the pilot.
[06:12] Jon: ok good. now about burst capacity — we do marketing pushes that spike traffic to 120 QPS for a few minutes. do you have burst options?
[06:20] Priya: yes, both Hosted and Dedicated can be configured with burst policies. Hosted has a pool for burst capacity and dedicated can enable burst nodes or autoscaling policies. the cost for burst is higher per-token if you keep idle capacity reserved; but short-lived burst reserved across a small percent of time usually is cheaper than pre-warming everything.
[06:41] [00:07:00] Evan: can you share an example-looking hourly cost estimate for a day with two 10-minute marketing spikes to 120 QPS and a baseline of 20 QPS?
[06:53] Alex: i'll populate the workbook but quick sketch: baseline 20 QPS sustained -> amortized cost X, spikes add delta mostly on completion tokens. with batching and prefix caching, spikes are somewhat cheapened for short prompt lengths. again spreadsheet will show per-hour and per-month view.
[07:10] Marisol: what about tooling — we need token-level cost breakdown and route-level dashboards.
[07:15] Alex: Redwood Console provides token-level breakdown, route/model dashboards, cost by token type and by route, and alerts on unit-cost regression. you can export CSVs for finance.
[07:26] Evan: any hidden fees for SSO or KMS integration on Private?
[07:31] Alex: KMS integrations and SSO (SAML/SCIM) are included in Private licensing. there's an initial setup fee for on-prem in some cases for air-gapped deployments but we'll call that out in SOW.
[07:44] Jon: what's typical contractual lead time for Dedicated vs Private?
[07:49] Priya: Dedicated (reserved capacity) can be spun up in a few days-weeks depending on capacity availability and your commit. Private, especially on-prem, takes longer — often 4-8 weeks for enterprise setups including KMS, networking, and acceptance testing.
[08:03] Evan: hmm our timeline for next quarter is tight — pilot must finish within 4 weeks so we can decide. Is that feasible?
[08:11] Alex: yes — a 2-week pilot + 1-week analysis + 1-week decisions is common. pilot scope: run benchmarks on representative prompts, measure p50/p90 latency, unit cost, and quality delta vs your current baseline.
[08:25] Marisol: baseline — we currently call an in-house 3B model on a single node for development; performance is poor on bursts and costs are unpredictable because of spot pricing. we think Redwood's hosted could give us consistent SLOs but worried about token burn.
[08:41] Priya: that's common. We'll show a comparison: current spot-based infra cost vs hosted per-token and vs dedicated per-node amortization. the caching and batching often close the gap.
[08:53] Marisol: how do you simulate our traffic? do you need a QPS histogram?
[08:57] Alex: yes please — sample prompt set (1000 examples) and a QPS histogram by hour or minute will let us produce realistic batch size distribution and projected cost.
[09:06] Evan: okay will send. can we also get a simple sensitivity table that shows cost as a function of prefix cache hit rate and batching window?
[09:13] Alex: yes will include in sheet: columns for cache hit % (40/60/80), batching windows (10/30/60ms), quant profiles (q8/q4) and resulting $/1k tokens & $/call.
[09:24] [00:10:00] Jon: on the topic of compliance — are audit logs granular enough for finance/ security teams? we need per-request audit trail kept for 90 days.
[09:33] Alex: Redwood Console audit logs include per-request metadata (timestamp, route, model version, tokens billed, request id). retention and export are configurable for Private and Dedicated; Hosted has default retention windows but enterprise add-ons can extend retention and S3 export. we'll include the retention options in the security pack.
[09:50] Marisol: do we get access to kernel perf traces or lower-level infra metrics for debugging?
[09:56] Priya: for Dedicated and Private, you can get more granular traces and we'll enable tracing hooks; hosted gives sampling-level traces due to multi-tenant constraints.
[10:06] Evan: let's talk numbers — Alex can you give an illustrative $/call estimate for our median call under hosted with q8 and 60% cache hit and batching window ~30ms?
[10:15] Alex: quick back-of-envelope: assume hosted rate $0.012 per 1k prompt tokens and $0.02 per 1k completion tokens (placeholder numbers in workbook). billed tokens per call ~110 -> that is ~0.00132 per call in prompt + 0.0012 completion = ~$0.0025 per call. scale to 1M calls/month -> ~$2.5k/month. if you add the spikes and longer tails cost goes up — spreadsheet will show full tail.
[10:46] Marisol: that's better than we feared. what's the delta if we run dedicated at a committed monthly price?
[10:52] Priya: depends on the node price and utilization. e.g., a dedicated 8xA100-like pool at reserve might be $Xk/month; at 60% utilization and same batching you'd amortize to ~$0.001-0.002 per call — often 20-40% lower than hosted at scale. again specific numbers in sheet.
[11:14] Evan: any cliffs where cost suddenly jumps? like if cache hit drops to 20%?
[11:18] Alex: yes cache hit drop is the biggest delta. our sensitivity table will highlight that. also very long completions are linear in tokens so long tail usage can blow budgets — we recommend token caps per route or guardrails.
[11:30] Jon: what about fallback policies when a hot path is saturated? we can't have user-facing errors.
[11:35] Priya: Redwood supports automatic fallbacks: you can route to a smaller/faster model or a cached response tier, or degrade noncritical features. fallbacks have configurable policies and we can train them for your critical flows.
[11:48] [00:12:00] Marisol: are there tooling hooks to mark a route as high-value so it always gets low-latency nodes?
[11:54] Alex: yes — route priority and tagging is supported and reflected in Console — you can set budgets per route, and our routing will keep those within low-latency pools.
[12:05] Evan: ok let's lock pilot goals: 1) validate p50/p90 under 100ms for top 3 query types, 2) achieve <$0.003 per median call, 3) no >5% quality regression vs baseline. sound reasonable?
[12:19] Marisol: yes but can we make the cost target a soft target? risk that spikes push us over.
[12:24] Alex: sure — we'll report variance and give recommendations on rate caps or route-level caps to enforce a hard spend guard.
[12:31] Evan: whats the SOW look like? length and deliverables?
[12:35] Alex: 2-week benchmark: provision environment (hosted/dedicated/ private as agreed), run prompt set, run load tests including spike scenarios, collect metrics, run quality evals, produce final report with cost sensitivity and recommendations. deliverables: benchmark corpus, raw traces, per-token cost model sheet, final report.
[12:56] Marisol: Who signs off on the pilot completion?
[13:00] Alex: typically Saffron will provide acceptance criteria signoff (per-criteria), and Redwood will present findings; we'll include acceptance checklist in SOW.
[13:08] Jon: fine. any blockers from our side? we need network access and sample prompts.
[13:12] Priya: we'll need the prompt set + a VPC peering if you want private networking for benchmarks; otherwise hosted benchmarks can run without peering.
[13:21] Evan: we'll do hosted pilot first then evaluate dedicated/private if results good.
[13:25] Alex: makes sense. we'll draft SOW for a hosted-first pilot with optional dedicated testing.
[13:31] [00:14:00] Marisol: small nit — can you include expected cost per 1k tokens at different quant levels? we want explicit #s for q8/q4.
[13:38] Alex: yes, sheet will have columns for q8/q4 and include delta percent.
[13:42] Evan: last question — do you support per-route token caps to prevent runaway costs?
[13:47] Priya: yes, route-level quotas and hard caps exist — you can also set alerts when cost thresholds approach.
[13:53] Alex: okay great — quick recap and action items: we'll share cost_model_v2.xlsx and the SOW draft by Tues (2026-02-16). Saffron will share prompts and QPS histograms by Wed (2026-02-17). Then we'll schedule kickoff for week of 2026-02-23.
[14:12] Evan: agreed. thanks Alex, Priya.
[14:15] Marisol: thanks. we'll aim to get the prompts over tomorrow.
[14:19] Jon: appreciate it.
[14:21] Alex: thanks everyone. I'll follow up with links to security docs and the sheet.
[14:25] [00:15:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (KV cache transcribed as 'K V cash'), timestamps approximate, filler words left in. Shared artifacts referenced: cost_model_v2.xlsx (link placeholder), SOW_draft_hosted-first.pdf (link placeholder), security_pack_redwood.pdf (link placeholder).
